title: And we're still fighting it.
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: Chris O'Brien opens the school year with a reflective, essayistic piece anchored in Ben Folds' song 'Still Fighting It,' using its lyrics about the pain of growing up to reframe the start of school as an emotionally weighty moment for both students and teachers. He reminds educators that every student walking through the doors was, just before, someone's 'whole world' at home — a parent fixing a collar, offering encouragement, lingering in the driveway before handing their child over for the day. O'Brien frames the teacher's responsibility as enormous: seven hours a day, 180 days a year, tasked with teaching, noticing, protecting, and knowing each child. He extends this into a call for empathy toward student behavior, illustrated through the example of a child who won't remove his backpack — reframed not as defiance but as a coping mechanism for something the child is quietly fighting.
points: Uses Ben Folds' song 'Still Fighting It' as a framing device for the emotional weight of a new school year.
Reminds teachers that every student was, minutes before, the center of someone's world at home.
Frames the teacher's daily responsibility (seven hours a day, 180 days) as an enormous trust placed in them by parents.
Reframes seemingly defiant student behavior (e.g., refusing to remove a backpack) as a sign of an unseen struggle.
Sets an emotionally reflective tone for the start of the school year, urging empathy over assumption.
quotes: Everybody knows, it hurts to grow up. And everybody does. ... And we're still fighting it.
It starts at breakfast, ordinary as anything, and turns into about the saddest and realest thing you can say to a kid you love. Growing up hurts.
And every student coming through your school doors was, forty-five minutes earlier, somebody's whole world standing in a kitchen.
Somebody fixed a collar. Somebody said you're gonna be great, buddy, and stood in the driveway a little longer than they needed to.
Then they handed their child to us. That's an enormous thing to be handed. Seven hours a day, a hundred and eighty days.
Teach them to read. Notice when something's wrong. Keep them safe. Keep them known. Send them home a little more than they came.
The one who won't take his backpack off all morning is not being defiant.
